description: Independent participant working on a solo project focused on software engineering, Python, data science, and AI/ML. Interested in building practical solutions using NASA's open data.
summary:
Urban Climate Blindspot is an exploratory geospatial project that investigates climate patterns and environmental observation gaps through a comparative case study of two African cities: Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso, and Lagos, Nigeria.

The project uses NASA POWER daily temperature data, including Earth skin temperature (TS) and 2-meter air temperature (T2M), to examine long-term patterns from 2003 to 2025. It combines this analysis with available ground-station records, land-cover information, and settlement geography to explore how environmental data availability and spatial context differ between the two locations.

The project includes a geospatial prototype that brings together selected datasets and allows users to explore the study areas and their environmental context. Its goal is to make data limitations more visible and encourage more careful, evidence-based investigation of climate patterns in cities that receive different levels of research attention.
details:
Project Overview

Urban Climate Blindspot is a geospatial research prototype designed to explore climate patterns and environmental observation gaps in African cities. The current study focuses on two locations: Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso, and Lagos, Nigeria.

Data and Methodology

The project uses NASA POWER daily time-series data for Earth skin temperature (TS) and 2-meter air temperature (T2M), covering 2003–2025. These variables are derived from MERRA-2 reanalysis and should not be interpreted as direct satellite thermal measurements or street-level air temperature observations.

Long-term temperature patterns are examined using annual averages and Theil–Sen slope estimates. Additional temporal analysis is used to investigate patterns within the available observation period.

To examine environmental data availability and geographical context, the project also uses:

  • NOAA GHCN-Daily records to assess the availability of nearby ground-station observations.
  • ESA WorldCover 2021 land-cover data for two fixed study windows around the selected locations.
  • GHSL GHS-SMOD settlement geography to provide urban-centre classification context.
  • Natural Earth geographic data for cartographic reference.

Prototype and Tools

The project includes a local geospatial atlas prototype that brings together selected datasets. It provides city-focused exploration, map navigation, year selection, and inspection of available spatial information.

The project uses Python for data processing and analysis, JavaScript for interface functionality, and JSON for structured processed data.

Why It Matters

Environmental research depends not only on the availability of climate observations but also on their spatial coverage, resolution, and reliability. A city may have limited nearby ground observations or may be represented by coarse-resolution reanalysis data that cannot capture neighbourhood-level conditions.

By comparing two cities with different geographical and observation contexts, Urban Climate Blindspot demonstrates why these limitations should be considered before drawing conclusions about urban climate patterns.

Limitations

This is an exploratory two-city case study, not a global assessment of African cities. The temperature trends are descriptive and do not establish causation. Ground-station availability is not equivalent to independent validation. The land-cover windows are not citywide assessments, and settlement classification boundaries are not municipal boundaries.

The prototype is intended to support further investigation rather than provide definitive conclusions about local climate drivers.
